screens.title: Introduction to Nodes: Geometry and Attributes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what a node really is in Houdini, why attributes are the language of geometry, and how a few common Surface Operators let you build procedural assets. A node takes data, applies a transformation under parameters you control, and outputs modified geometry. That chaining — connecting outputs to inputs — is how small operations become complex models. Attributes like position, normals, and color live on points, vertices, and primitives and carry information through every node. We will practice simple SOPs: creating geometry, grouping faces, extruding to add depth, and merging pieces into a single mesh. You will also learn to inspect results with the Geometry Spreadsheet and visualize normals in the viewport so you can check what each node produced. By the end, you’ll understand the procedural pattern: generate, select, modify, combine, and inspect. That pattern is the same whether you build a wall piece or a game-ready prop. As you start, notice how small parameter changes ripple downstream — that’s the power and responsibility of procedural node design.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Introduction to Nodes
Introduction to Nodes: Geometry and Attributes
How SOPs, attributes, and node chains shape procedural geometry
In this lesson

Explore how nodes accept inputs, expose parameters, and output geometry. Learn common SOPs and how attributes like P, N, and Cd flow through a node chain.

Why it matters
Procedural workflows let you iterate quickly and create reusable, parametric assets for games and VFX.
What you'll practice
Creating a box, grouping faces, extruding for a window recess, merging pieces, and inspecting attributes.
Visual concept
Data flows through node chains; attributes ride on geometry.
Explore Key Topics
Nodes & Chaining
A node performs one operation; connect them to build complex results.
Attributes
Data like P, N, and Cd live on geometry and move through the network.
SOP Toolbox
Transform, Group, PolyExtrude, and Merge are core building blocks you will use often.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these exercises you will be able to explain the internal structure of a node, including the concept of inputs, outputs, and editable parameters. You will be able to create and chain nodes in the Network Editor to form a sequence of operations that builds geometry progressively. You will also be able to identify and use core attributes: position, normals, and color, and inspect them in the Geometry Spreadsheet. Finally, you will apply this knowledge using basic SOPs to manipulate geometry — transforming shapes, grouping components, extruding faces, and merging streams — so you can build a modular object like a wall with a window recess. Each objective is focused on practical skill: explanation, creation, identification, and application. We will verify competency by inspecting node outputs, observing how attributes change after operations, and completing the hands-on wall build. Notice that these objectives combine conceptual understanding with procedural practice so you gain both mental models and repeatable techniques.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen translates the chapter goals into practice tasks and quick verification steps. You will build a modular wall piece by creating a Geometry node, generating a box primitive, and positioning it with parameters. Then you will create a Group to select window faces and use PolyExtrude to carve a recess. You will observe the Geometry Spreadsheet at different nodes to see changes in point counts and attributes like P and Cd. To verify your work, set the display flag on intermediate nodes and confirm that selection groups target the intended primitives. A useful habit is to inspect normals after extrusions to ensure surface orientation is correct for shading. We will also review common errors: incorrect wiring that leaves nodes disconnected, applying operations in the wrong order, or forgetting to reference the named group. These practice steps and checks give you a reliable workflow to iterate and validate procedural geometry.

keyIdea.text: Hands-on tasks and quick inspections help verify node wiring, group selection, attribute propagation, and order-of-operations.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Practice & Verification
Practice Task
  1. Create a Geometry node named modular_wall and dive inside.
  2. Add a Box SOP and set Size to 4,3,0.2 and Center Y to 1.5.
  3. Create a Group SOP to select window faces and name it window_faces.
  4. Use PolyExtrude on that group with a negative distance to create a recess.
Checkpoints: display flags, Geometry Spreadsheet, viewport normals.
Verification Tips
  • Set display flags on intermediate nodes to inspect incremental changes.
  • Open Geometry Spreadsheet to compare point and primitive counts before/after extrusion.
  • Visualize normals to confirm correct face orientation after operations.
Common mistake: leaving nodes unconnected or applying operations in the wrong order.
Why this matters
Verification is how you build trust in a procedural network. Small checks prevent compounding errors downstream and keep assets predictable for reuse.
Mini-mnemonic
Generate → Group → Modify → Inspect → Merge

screens.title: What is a Node?
screens.narratorSegment: A node is a discrete operator that takes data, applies a parameterized operation, and emits modified data. Think of each node as a single recipe step: it expects an input, has controls you can tweak, and produces an output that other nodes can consume. This simple model makes Houdini predictable and modular. For example, a Box SOP does one thing: it generates a box primitive with size and center parameters. A Transform SOP does one thing: it adjusts positions based on translate, rotate, and scale parameters. When you internalize nodes as atomic operations, you gain clarity about how changes propagate: altering a parameter on an upstream node will change the inputs downstream. A common misconception is to treat nodes as layers of a final model rather than steps in a process. That leads learners to duplicate work or to overwrite earlier procedural decisions. Instead, use nodes to encode intent — create geometry, select the area to affect, apply a targeted operation, then inspect. Finally, a node's parameters are not 'magic'; they map directly to the underlying mathematical transform or selection rule. Practice by creating a Box, adjusting its size values, and watching how the generated points — the P attribute — update in the Geometry Spreadsheet. What single step could you isolate into its own node to make your network clearer?

keyIdea.text: A node is an atomic, parameterized operator: input data in, processed data out; chain them to build behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is a Node?
Definition
A single, focused operator

Nodes accept inputs, expose parameters, process data, and send results downstream. Treat them like steps in a recipe rather than layers of a finished model.

Concrete example
Create a Box SOP and change its Size parameters. The P attribute for each generated point updates to the new coordinates.
Common misconception
Treating nodes as final layers can hide the sequence of operations and make debugging harder.
Key Takeaway

Design networks as small steps with clear parameters so changes remain predictable and debuggable.

Visual aid
Node card examples
Box
Generates geometry with Size and Center parameters.
Transform
Shifts points using translate, rotate, and scale values.
Group
Creates named selections used by later nodes.
Merge
Combines multiple geometry streams into one.

screens.title: Inputs, Outputs, and Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: A node's inputs, outputs, and parameters form a simple contract: inputs are the data it expects, parameters define how it processes that data, and outputs are the resulting geometry and attributes. Inputs often include geometry streams carrying points, primitives, and attached attributes. Parameters expose the node's configurable behavior — for instance, a PolyExtrude exposes a distance parameter that determines how far faces move along their normals. Outputs return the modified geometry and any new attributes created by the node. When you wire nodes, you are deciding which output becomes the input for the next operation. A useful concrete habit is to inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet at each stage: compare point counts and key attributes before and after a node to see exactly what changed. A common mistake is to assume parameters only affect appearance; many parameters change topology or attribute layout, which affects downstream nodes. For example, extruding faces can add points and primitives, so a later node that references a named group must still match the new topology. Ask yourself: how will changing this parameter affect the attribute layout and downstream node expectations?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Inputs, Outputs, Parameters
Contract

Inputs: geometry and attributes. Parameters: control behavior. Outputs: modified geometry and attributes. Parameters can change topology and attribute layout.

Example
PolyExtrude with negative distance reduces front-face position along normals and creates additional primitives, increasing point count visible in the spreadsheet.
Misconception
Parameters only change appearance. In fact, many change topology and attributes, which downstream nodes may rely on.
Key Takeaway

Always inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet after parameter changes to verify topology and attribute changes.

Step-by-step check
1. Inspect inputs
Open the Geometry Spreadsheet on the input node to see P, N, Cd and counts.
2. Change parameters
Adjust distance, translate, or selection, and observe immediate viewport changes.
3. Inspect outputs
Compare the Spreadsheet to see how attributes and counts were affected.

screens.title: SOPs: Geometry Nodes at Work
screens.narratorSegment: SOPs, or Surface Operators, are the nodes you use inside a Geometry container to manipulate the raw components of a mesh: points, primitives, and edges. Each SOP focuses on a specific kind of manipulation. A Box SOP generates geometry with points and primitives. A Transform SOP changes point positions. A Group SOP creates named selections that let later nodes act on only part of the geometry. Merge brings multiple streams together in a single output. Understanding how these components map to geometry concepts matters because some SOPs operate on points, others on primitives, and selection modes determine what exactly will be affected. For instance, if you create a group of primitives and then run a PolyExtrude that expects a primitive group, the operation will extrude faces; if you accidentally made a point group instead, the extrude may not behave as expected. A good practice is to annotate groups with clear names and use the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm the group membership. Think of SOPs as a small toolbox: pick the right tool for the job and verify that the selection type matches the operation.

keyIdea.title: SOP architecture
keyIdea.text: SOPs operate on points, primitives, or edges; match selection type and operation to avoid unexpected results.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › SOPs: Geometry Nodes
Core SOPs
Points, Primitives, Edges

Know which SOP operates on which component and ensure your groups match that selection type. Using the correct selection type prevents unintended consequences during operations like extrusion.

Box
Generates points and primitives for a simple cube or flat box.
Transform
Manipulates point positions to move, rotate, or scale geometry.
PolyExtrude
Extrudes selected primitives, creating new faces and changing topology.
Selection & Verification
Use the Group SOP to name collections of points or primitives. Always confirm group membership in the Geometry Spreadsheet or viewport highlighting before running topology-changing nodes.
Example workflow
Create Box → Group front-face primitives as window_faces → PolyExtrude using window_faces to make a recess.
Pitfall
Selecting the wrong component type for a group will make some SOPs appear to do nothing; confirm selection mode before applying.

screens.title: Common SOPs Compared
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the purpose of frequently used SOPs helps you pick the right tool quickly. Transform operates on point positions to move, scale, or rotate geometry. Use Transform for simple translations or when you need to change local transforms without adding topology. Merge combines multiple geometry streams; use Merge when you have separate pieces — for example a wall and a window frame — that must be processed together. PolyExtrude changes topology by extruding selected primitives to add depth; use it when you need new faces, thickness, or architectural detail. Group does not modify geometry directly; instead it creates named selections so subsequent SOPs apply to those specific components. An important practical contrast: Transform is topology-preserving, whereas PolyExtrude is topology-changing. That distinction is crucial because topology changes affect downstream attribute counts and group membership. Practice selecting the same faces and applying Transform versus PolyExtrude to see the difference in the Geometry Spreadsheet. Which nodes will you pick when you need a non-destructive offset vs. a topology-altering shape change? Common SOPs Compared means transform preserves topology, polyextrude creates new geometry, merge consolidates streams, and group scopes operations.. In practical terms, transform, merge, polyextrude, group — when and why to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Common SOPs Compared
At-a-glance
Transform
Topology-preserving position, rotate, scale.
PolyExtrude
Topology-changing extrusion of selected primitives.
Merge
Combine multiple inputs into a single stream.
Group
Create named selections for targeted operations.
Practical example
Create a Box for the wall, Group the front face primitives as window_faces, use PolyExtrude on window_faces with a negative distance to carve a recess, create a separate Box for the window frame, Transform that box into place, then Merge the frame with the wall to produce one object.
Check the spreadsheet
Compare point counts and primitive IDs before and after PolyExtrude to confirm topology changes.

screens.title: Attributes: P, N, Cd and where they live
screens.narratorSegment: Attributes are variables attached directly to geometry components. They are how you store and pass information through a node network. The most fundamental attribute is P, the position vector holding x, y, z coordinates for each point. N is the normal vector that indicates surface orientation and is critical for lighting and extrusion directions. Cd stores color as an r, g, b vector and can live per-point or per-primitive depending on how you set it. Attributes can exist on points, vertices, primitives, or the whole detail. Choosing where to store an attribute matters: point attributes follow points when topology changes, while primitive attributes describe faces and remain tied to those primitives. A frequent learner error is assuming an attribute exists where you expect it; always verify in the Geometry Spreadsheet which attribute exists on which component tab. A practical example: when you extrude faces using PolyExtrude, N guides the extrusion direction; if normals are incorrect or missing, the extrusion may collapse or push inward unexpectedly. Think about attributes as data columns in a table — they give meaning to geometry beyond its raw coordinates.

keyIdea.title: Attribute roles
keyIdea.text: P stores positions, N stores normals for direction, Cd stores color; attributes live on points, vertices, primitives, or detail and affect behaviors differently.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Attributes: P, N, Cd
Attribute breakdown
P — Position
Vector of three floats defining point location. Visible in the Points tab of the spreadsheet.
N — Normal
Surface direction used for shading and directional operations like extrusion.
Cd — Color
Diffuse color stored as r, g, b; can live per-point or per-primitive.
Where attributes live
Attributes can be stored on points, vertices, primitives, or detail. The storage location determines how attributes behave when topology changes. For example, point attributes move with points, while primitive attributes stay tied to faces.
Practical check
Open Geometry Spreadsheet and verify which tab (Points, Primitives) shows P, N, or Cd after each node.
Tip
If an operation behaves strangely, check whether the expected attribute exists on the component type the SOP operates on.

screens.title: Inspecting Attributes in the Geometry Spreadsheet
screens.narratorSegment: The Geometry Spreadsheet is your primary debugging tool for understanding what data lives on your geometry at each step. It presents attribute columns for the selected component type: Points, Vertices, Primitives, or Detail. To inspect positions, open the Points tab and look at the P column; you will see three floats per row describing each point’s coordinates. If you are checking normals used for extrusion, verify the N column and make sure vectors point outward for the faces you intend to extrude. For color, check the Cd column under the Primitives or Points tab depending on where it’s stored. A common inspection workflow is to toggle the display flag on a node, open the Spreadsheet, and compare counts and attribute values before and after a node that modifies topology. If you see unexpected zeros or missing columns, that indicates the node did not produce the attribute you expected. For example, running PolyExtrude may increase point count; if a downstream node assumes a fixed point index, that assumption breaks. Regularly comparing the Spreadsheet across nodes prevents subtle attribute mismatches that cause rendering and simulation errors.

keyIdea.title: Spreadsheet use
keyIdea.text: Use the Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect attribute columns and topology changes after each node to catch mismatches early.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Geometry Spreadsheet
Reading the table

Open Points, Primitives, or Detail tabs to see attribute columns. P shows coordinates; N shows normals; Cd shows color. Compare counts and values across nodes to identify changes.

Example inspection
Before PolyExtrude: 24 points. After PolyExtrude: 32 points. Verify P values for new points and N directions for extruded faces.
Debug tip
Missing Cd column means the color attribute was not created. Check upstream nodes that should add attributes and ensure they're set to write to the correct component type.
Quick checks
  • Toggle node display flags and compare Spreadsheet rows and columns.
  • Confirm attribute types (float, vector) and number of components.
  • Note topology changes: point and primitive counts should match expected transformations.
Key Takeaway

Treat the Spreadsheet as a truth table for your network; it prevents assumptions about attribute presence and topology.

screens.title: Node Chaining and Order of Operations
screens.narratorSegment: The order in which you chain nodes dictates the final geometry. Nodes form a pipeline: each node receives the output of its predecessors. That sequence is not interchangeable because many nodes depend on the current topology and attributes. For example, applying a Transform before PolyExtrude produces a different result than extruding first and then transforming. If you extrude first, new points and faces are created and then transformed as a group. If you transform first, the extrusion sees the original topology and normals and may produce a different offset. A practical mental model is to read the network like a recipe: first mix, then bake, then glaze. In Houdini terms: generate geometry, select with Group, modify with PolyExtrude, then combine with Merge. A useful debugging habit is to set the display flag on intermediate nodes to see incremental effects and to comment or label nodes with a short description of intent. Remember that reordering nodes changes both geometry and attribute history, so plan sequences with the eventual use in mind — for example, whether the final asset needs consistent point indices for downstream tools or dynamic attributes for shading.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Node Chaining & Order
Chain example
Box → Group(window_faces) → PolyExtrude(window_faces) → Transform → Merge(frame). Each step builds on the last, and changing order alters results.
Try this
Apply Transform before PolyExtrude and then after to compare differences in point positions and extrusion behavior.
Common error
Connecting the wrong output or leaving a node unconnected often results in stale geometry being used downstream.
Verification strip
Display flags
Set the display flag on a node to preview that node's output. Use this to confirm each step before chaining more operations.
Label nodes
Add short labels describing intent so you remember why a node was placed in the network and can reorder safely.

screens.title: Group SOP: Select with Purpose

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Group SOP
Purpose

Use groups to name and isolate parts of geometry for targeted operations. Group Type must match the type of components you intend to select.

Example
Create a primitive group named window_faces and reference it in PolyExtrude to recess those faces only.
Pitfall
Creating the wrong component type for the group (points vs. primitives) will cause later nodes to appear to do nothing.
Workflow
  1. Choose Group Type: Points, Vertices, or Primitives.
  2. Select using viewport picks, bounding regions, or attribute filters.
  3. Name the group clearly and confirm membership in the Spreadsheet.
  4. Reference the group in downstream nodes' Group parameter.
Key Takeaway

Use groups to scope operations and keep networks readable and reusable.

screens.title: Build: Modular Wall with Window Recess
screens.narratorSegment: Now we will walk the full hands-on build as a single, repeatable sequence. Start a new scene, create a Geometry node and dive inside. Add a Box SOP and set its Size to 4,3,0.2 and Center Y to 1.5 so it sits on the ground. Immediately set the display flag to view the box. Next add a Group SOP and set Group Type to Primitives. Name it window_faces and select the front faces in the viewport for the window area. Confirm membership in the Geometry Spreadsheet to ensure you selected primitives. After that, add a PolyExtrude SOP, reference window_faces in its Group parameter, and set Distance to a small negative value like -0.1 to push faces inward and create the recess. Reduce Divisions to 1 for a clean result. To create a frame, add another Box SOP, adjust its Size to match a frame profile, and use Transform to position it in the recess. Finally, add a Merge SOP to combine the wall and frame into one stream. Use the Spreadsheet and display flags between steps to verify topology and attributes. This stepwise pipeline highlights how each node builds on the prior one.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Modular Wall Build
Step-by-step
  1. Create a Geometry node named modular_wall and dive inside.
  2. Add Box SOP: Size = 4,3,0.2; Center Y = 1.5. Set display flag.
  3. Add Group SOP: Type = Primitives, Name = window_faces; select front faces in viewport.
  4. Add PolyExtrude: Group = window_faces; Distance = -0.1; Divisions = 1; set display flag.
  5. Create another Box for window frame, adjust Size, then Transform to place it into the recess.
  6. Add Merge SOP to combine wall and frame into a single output stream.
  7. Open Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect P, N, and counts after key steps.
Concrete checks
Checkpoint
After Group, confirm window_faces appears in Primitive tab. After PolyExtrude, confirm increased point/primitive counts.
Tip
Use a negative extrusion distance to push inward for a recess. Keep Divisions low for a clean cut.
Mistake to avoid
Merging before positioning the frame can make the transform harder; position before merge to preserve local transforms.
Key Takeaway

Follow the pipeline and verify after each topology-changing node to keep the network predictable.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: As you build networks, you will encounter predictable mistakes. The first is disconnected or incorrectly-wired nodes. A node that is not connected, or wired to the wrong output, will feed stale geometry downstream. Verify wiring visually and by setting display flags. Second, topology surprises occur when a node changes point or primitive counts in a way you didn't expect; always inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet after topology-changing nodes like PolyExtrude. Third, attribute mismatches happen when downstream nodes expect an attribute that was never created or was created on a different component type. To prevent this, name groups clearly and confirm attribute presence in the appropriate tab. Best practices include: labeling nodes with intent, using small composable groups, checking intermediates with the display flag, and relying on the Spreadsheet for exact values. Treat each node as a documented step in a pipeline — when you revisit a network, descriptive node names and tidy groups make it far easier to debug and extend. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what a node really is in Houdini, why attributes are the language of geometry, and how a few common Surface Operators let you build procedural assets. A node takes data, applies a transformation under parameters you control, and outputs modified geometry. That chaining — connecting outputs to inputs — is how small operations become complex models. Attributes like position, normals, and color live on points, vertices, and primitives and carry information through every node. We will practice simple SOPs: creating geometry, grouping faces, extruding to add depth, and merging pieces into a single mesh. You will also learn to inspect results with the Geometry Spreadsheet and visualize normals in the viewport so you can check what each node produced. By the end, you’ll understand the procedural pattern: generate, select, modify, combine, and inspect. That pattern is the same whether you build a wall piece or a game-ready prop. As you start, notice how small parameter changes ripple downstream — that’s the power and responsibility of procedural node design.

By the end of these exercises you will be able to explain the internal structure of a node, including the concept of inputs, outputs, and editable parameters. You will be able to create and chain nodes in the Network Editor to form a sequence of operations that builds geometry progressively. You will also be able to identify and use core attributes: position, normals, and color, and inspect them in the Geometry Spreadsheet. Finally, you will apply this knowledge using basic SOPs to manipulate geometry — transforming shapes, grouping components, extruding faces, and merging streams — so you can build a modular object like a wall with a window recess. Each objective is focused on practical skill: explanation, creation, identification, and application. We will verify competency by inspecting node outputs, observing how attributes change after operations, and completing the hands-on wall build. Notice that these objectives combine conceptual understanding with procedural practice so you gain both mental models and repeatable techniques.

This second objectives screen translates the chapter goals into practice tasks and quick verification steps. You will build a modular wall piece by creating a Geometry node, generating a box primitive, and positioning it with parameters. Then you will create a Group to select window faces and use PolyExtrude to carve a recess. You will observe the Geometry Spreadsheet at different nodes to see changes in point counts and attributes like P and Cd. To verify your work, set the display flag on intermediate nodes and confirm that selection groups target the intended primitives. A useful habit is to inspect normals after extrusions to ensure surface orientation is correct for shading. We will also review common errors: incorrect wiring that leaves nodes disconnected, applying operations in the wrong order, or forgetting to reference the named group. These practice steps and checks give you a reliable workflow to iterate and validate procedural geometry.

A node is a discrete operator that takes data, applies a parameterized operation, and emits modified data. Think of each node as a single recipe step: it expects an input, has controls you can tweak, and produces an output that other nodes can consume. This simple model makes Houdini predictable and modular. For example, a Box SOP does one thing: it generates a box primitive with size and center parameters. A Transform SOP does one thing: it adjusts positions based on translate, rotate, and scale parameters. When you internalize nodes as atomic operations, you gain clarity about how changes propagate: altering a parameter on an upstream node will change the inputs downstream. A common misconception is to treat nodes as layers of a final model rather than steps in a process. That leads learners to duplicate work or to overwrite earlier procedural decisions. Instead, use nodes to encode intent — create geometry, select the area to affect, apply a targeted operation, then inspect. Finally, a node's parameters are not 'magic'; they map directly to the underlying mathematical transform or selection rule. Practice by creating a Box, adjusting its size values, and watching how the generated points — the P attribute — update in the Geometry Spreadsheet. What single step could you isolate into its own node to make your network clearer?

A node's inputs, outputs, and parameters form a simple contract: inputs are the data it expects, parameters define how it processes that data, and outputs are the resulting geometry and attributes. Inputs often include geometry streams carrying points, primitives, and attached attributes. Parameters expose the node's configurable behavior — for instance, a PolyExtrude exposes a distance parameter that determines how far faces move along their normals. Outputs return the modified geometry and any new attributes created by the node. When you wire nodes, you are deciding which output becomes the input for the next operation. A useful concrete habit is to inspect the Geometry Spreadsheet at each stage: compare point counts and key attributes before and after a node to see exactly what changed. A common mistake is to assume parameters only affect appearance; many parameters change topology or attribute layout, which affects downstream nodes. For example, extruding faces can add points and primitives, so a later node that references a named group must still match the new topology. Ask yourself: how will changing this parameter affect the attribute layout and downstream node expectations?

SOPs, or Surface Operators, are the nodes you use inside a Geometry container to manipulate the raw components of a mesh: points, primitives, and edges. Each SOP focuses on a specific kind of manipulation. A Box SOP generates geometry with points and primitives. A Transform SOP changes point positions. A Group SOP creates named selections that let later nodes act on only part of the geometry. Merge brings multiple streams together in a single output. Understanding how these components map to geometry concepts matters because some SOPs operate on points, others on primitives, and selection modes determine what exactly will be affected. For instance, if you create a group of primitives and then run a PolyExtrude that expects a primitive group, the operation will extrude faces; if you accidentally made a point group instead, the extrude may not behave as expected. A good practice is to annotate groups with clear names and use the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm the group membership. Think of SOPs as a small toolbox: pick the right tool for the job and verify that the selection type matches the operation.

Understanding the purpose of frequently used SOPs helps you pick the right tool quickly. Transform operates on point positions to move, scale, or rotate geometry. Use Transform for simple translations or when you need to change local transforms without adding topology. Merge combines multiple geometry streams; use Merge when you have separate pieces — for example a wall and a window frame — that must be processed together. PolyExtrude changes topology by extruding selected primitives to add depth; use it when you need new faces, thickness, or architectural detail. Group does not modify geometry directly; instead it creates named selections so subsequent SOPs apply to those specific components. An important practical contrast: Transform is topology-preserving, whereas PolyExtrude is topology-changing. That distinction is crucial because topology changes affect downstream attribute counts and group membership. Practice selecting the same faces and applying Transform versus PolyExtrude to see the difference in the Geometry Spreadsheet. Which nodes will you pick when you need a non-destructive offset vs. a topology-altering shape change? In practical terms, transform, merge, polyextrude, group — when and why to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Attributes are variables attached directly to geometry components. They are how you store and pass information through a node network. The most fundamental attribute is P, the position vector holding x, y, z coordinates for each point. N is the normal vector that indicates surface orientation and is critical for lighting and extrusion directions. Cd stores color as an r, g, b vector and can live per-point or per-primitive depending on how you set it. Attributes can exist on points, vertices, primitives, or the whole detail. Choosing where to store an attribute matters: point attributes follow points when topology changes, while primitive attributes describe faces and remain tied to those primitives. A frequent learner error is assuming an attribute exists where you expect it; always verify in the Geometry Spreadsheet which attribute exists on which component tab. A practical example: when you extrude faces using PolyExtrude, N guides the extrusion direction; if normals are incorrect or missing, the extrusion may collapse or push inward unexpectedly. Think about attributes as data columns in a table — they give meaning to geometry beyond its raw coordinates.

The Geometry Spreadsheet is your primary debugging tool for understanding what data lives on your geometry at each step. It presents attribute columns for the selected component type: Points, Vertices, Primitives, or Detail. To inspect positions, open the Points tab and look at the P column; you will see three floats per row describing each point’s coordinates. If you are checking normals used for extrusion, verify the N column and make sure vectors point outward for the faces you intend to extrude. For color, check the Cd column under the Primitives or Points tab depending on where it’s stored. A common inspection workflow is to toggle the display flag on a node, open the Spreadsheet, and compare counts and attribute values before and after a node that modifies topology. If you see unexpected zeros or missing columns, that indicates the node did not produce the attribute you expected. For example, running PolyExtrude may increase point count; if a downstream node assumes a fixed point index, that assumption breaks. Regularly comparing the Spreadsheet across nodes prevents subtle attribute mismatches that cause rendering and simulation errors.

The order in which you chain nodes dictates the final geometry. Nodes form a pipeline: each node receives the output of its predecessors. That sequence is not interchangeable because many nodes depend on the current topology and attributes. For example, applying a Transform before PolyExtrude produces a different result than extruding first and then transforming. If you extrude first, new points and faces are created and then transformed as a group. If you transform first, the extrusion sees the original topology and normals and may produce a different offset. A practical mental model is to read the network like a recipe: first mix, then bake, then glaze. In Houdini terms: generate geometry, select with Group, modify with PolyExtrude, then combine with Merge. A useful debugging habit is to set the display flag on intermediate nodes to see incremental effects and to comment or label nodes with a short description of intent. Remember that reordering nodes changes both geometry and attribute history, so plan sequences with the eventual use in mind — for example, whether the final asset needs consistent point indices for downstream tools or dynamic attributes for shading.
